title: Why averages are not enough: measures of variability
summary: Two data sets can share the same mean, median and mode and still look completely different. Measures of variability tell you how spread out the data is.

chunks.heading: Same average, different spread
chunks.explanation_md:
The deck asks a direct question: **are mean, median and mode sufficient?**

Look at the two suppliers. **Supplier-1** is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. **Supplier-2** is 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8.

For both sets the **mean = median = mode = 6**. Yet the picture is very different. In Supplier-1 the **data are spread out** (from 1 to 11). In Supplier-2 the **data are clustered together** (from 4 to 8).

So an average alone cannot tell you which set is more consistent. You need a second number that measures spread.

key_terms.meaning: How far apart the data values are, shown by the supplier data sets that share an average of 6 but differ in spread.

chunks.exam_line: Data sets with the same mean, median and mode (all 6 for the two suppliers) can still differ: one is spread out, the other is clustered together.

chunks.heading: Why we measure variability
chunks.explanation_md:
The professor says it is often **desirable to consider measures of variability (dispersion) as well as measures of central tendency**.

His example: when choosing **supplier A or supplier B**, look not only at the **average delivery time** of each, but also at the **variability in delivery time** of each. A supplier who is on time on average but sometimes very late is a different risk from one who is steady.

The deck covers five measures of variability:
1. **Range**
2. **Interquartile Range**
3. **Variance**
4. **Standard Deviation**
5. **Coefficient of Variation**

key_terms.meaning: Numbers that describe how spread out the data is, also called dispersion: range, interquartile range, variance, standard deviation and coefficient of variation.

questions.stem: Using the two supplier data sets, state their ranges and say which supplier is more spread out.
questions.model_answer_md:
Range = largest value - smallest value.

- **Supplier-1:** 11 - 1 = **10**
- **Supplier-2:** 8 - 4 = **4**

Supplier-1 has the larger range, so its data are **more spread out**, even though both have mean = median = mode = 6.

questions.stem: A manager says a supplier with an average delivery time of 6 days is 'reliable'. Use the deck's idea to challenge this in a few lines.
questions.model_answer_md:
An **average alone does not show reliability**. The deck's two supplier sets both have a mean, median and mode of 6, but Supplier-1 is spread out from 1 to 11 while Supplier-2 is clustered from 4 to 8.

A supplier who is sometimes very early and sometimes very late is a different risk from one who is steady. So the manager must also look at the **variability in delivery time** (for example the range or standard deviation) before judging reliability.

questions.stem: Explain why mean, median and mode are not sufficient to describe a data set. Support your answer with the two supplier data sets and show how the range separates them.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Introduction.** Mean, median and mode describe the centre of the data. They say nothing about how far the values stretch around that centre, so two data sets can look identical on all three and still behave very differently.

**Example from the deck.** Supplier-1: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11. Supplier-2: 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8. For both, **mean = median = mode = 6**. On the dot plots Supplier-1 is **spread out** and Supplier-2 is **clustered together**.

**What separates them.** A measure of variability does. The simplest is the range: Supplier-1 = 11 - 1 = 10; Supplier-2 = 8 - 4 = 4. The larger range shows Supplier-1 is more spread out.

**Why it matters.** When choosing a supplier we should consider not only the average delivery time but also the **variability in delivery time**. A steady supplier is easier to plan around.

**Measures available.** Range, interquartile range, variance, standard deviation and coefficient of variation.

**Conclusion.** Always report a measure of centre together with a measure of spread.

questions.stem: Compare Supplier-1 and Supplier-2 using range and sample standard deviation, and give a managerial recommendation on which supplier to prefer for dependable delivery.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Data.** Supplier-1: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 (n = 12). Supplier-2: 4, 5, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7, 7, 7, 8 (n = 12). Both have a mean of 6 (each total is 72).

**Range.** Supplier-1: 11 - 1 = 10. Supplier-2: 8 - 4 = 4.

**Sample standard deviation**, s = √[Σ(x - x̄)² / (n - 1)].
- Supplier-1: squared deviations 25, 16, 9, 4, 1, 0, 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 add to 110. s² = 110 / 11 = 10, so **s = 3.16**.
- Supplier-2: squared deviations add to 14. s² = 14 / 11 = 1.27, so **s = 1.13**.

**Interpretation.** With the same mean, median and mode (6), Supplier-1 has both the larger range (10 against 4) and the larger standard deviation (3.16 against 1.13). Its delivery times are far less consistent.

**Recommendation.** Prefer **Supplier-2** for dependable delivery because its times are clustered close to the average of 6. The average alone could not show this.
